---
order: 6
unit: you
title: Pressure and tricks
summary: "Some messages and ads are built to make you act before you think: a countdown, a prize you never entered, 'only 3 left', 'everyone has it'. Pressure to hurry is a sign to slow down. Stop, check where it really comes from, and ask someone before you click, pay, or give a password or code. Nobody real minds you checking."
language: science
shape: 5e
hook: "A pop-up in Leo's game flashes: 'You've WON 10,000 free gems! Claim in the next 60 seconds!' His finger is already on the button. What should he do first?"
---
Leo, Grace and every message here are made up. You do not need to say what has happened to you.

## Engage: why the hurry?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a guess: a countdown is there to stop you thinking, not because the deadline is real."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Why does the pop-up give Leo only 60 seconds?"
  options: ["So he clicks before he stops to think or ask anyone", "Because the gems really run out", "Because games are fast"]
  actual: "So he acts before thinking. A countdown is one of the oldest tricks: hurry stops you checking. A real offer will still be there after you ask."
```

## Explore: spot the push

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting messages by the push they use shows a short list of tricks that come back again and again."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "What push does each message use?"
  options: ["Hurry", "A prize you didn't enter", "Everyone has it", "No push"]
  items:
    - ["'Only 2 minutes left to claim your skin!'", "Hurry", "A countdown to stop you thinking."]
    - ["'Congratulations! You've been picked to win a tablet!'", "A prize you didn't enter", "You can't win something you never entered."]
    - ["'All your friends have the gold pass. Don't be left out.'", "Everyone has it", "It makes you feel left out, so you act."]
    - ["'Your library book is due back on Monday.'", "No push", "A real reminder, nothing asked, no hurry."]
    - ["'Last chance! Offer ends tonight!'", "Hurry", "Hurry again."]
    - ["'Your class photo is ready to view on the school site.'", "No push", "Expected, from a place you know, nothing asked."]
```

Was your guess right? A few pushes come back again and again: **hurry**, **a prize you didn't enter**, and **everyone has it**. Spotting the push is the first step.

## Explain: slow down, check, ask

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Naming the habit: pressure means slow down. The planted mistake is treating a rush as a sign it's real."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#grace"
      text: "Grace gets a message in a game. Click the line where her thinking first goes wrong."
      answer: 2
      fault: logic
      misconception: rush-means-real
      explain: "Line 2: Grace thinks the countdown means she must act now. Pressure to hurry is the sign to slow down. A real offer would still be there after she asked."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A message asks Leo for his password 'to send the gems'. What should he do?"
      options: ["Never give it; close the message and ask a trusted adult", "Give it, because the gems are free", "Give it but change it later", "Give only half of it"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Nothing real needs your password to give you something.", "Someone could use it straight away.", "Any part of it helps someone guess the rest."]
      explain: "Passwords and codes are only typed into the real app or site, never sent to anyone. Real companies don't ask for them in a message."
```

When something pushes you to hurry, that's the moment to **slow down**:

1. **Stop.** Take your finger off the button. A real offer can wait.
2. **Check.** Who is it really from? Did you enter, order or ask for this?
3. **Ask.** Show a trusted adult before you click, pay, or give a password, a code or personal details.

Never send a password or a code to anyone, even someone friendly. Nobody real minds you checking. How computers work has more on messages that pretend to be someone you trust: [Spot the phish](../../../systems/cyber/phishing/).

## Elaborate: an older inbox

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Years 7 and 8: the same pushes in email, with a link that says one thing and goes somewhere else."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#inbox", height: 620 }
hint: ["Check where each link really goes before you decide.", "Look for hurry, a prize, a request for a password, and an address that isn't quite right."]
check: { type: board, text: "Mark each message in Ava's made-up inbox Safe or Report.", when: "a = n", explain: "The prize and the 'account closed today' messages use hurry and ask for a password; the second also uses a lookalike address. The club and teacher messages ask for nothing and their links match." }
```

## Evaluate: what would you do?

```step
stage: info
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "An ad says 'Everyone in Year 6 has these shoes. Only 3 left!' What is the best first move?"
      options: ["Notice the two pushes, close it, and decide later with someone", "Buy them before they're gone", "Share it with friends so they can get some too", "Click to see if it's true"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "'Only 3 left' and 'everyone has it' are there to make you hurry.", "Sharing passes the push on to your friends.", "Clicking is what the ad wants. Close it and come back later if you still want them."]
      explain: "Spot the pushes (hurry and everyone has it), then slow down."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can spot hurry, a prize I didn't enter and 'everyone has it', and I know to stop, check and ask." }
```

**A private think** (just for you): who would you show a message like this to?

```teacher
summary: "Students sort made-up messages by the push they use (hurry, a prize
  you didn't enter, everyone has it, no push), find the mistake in treating a
  countdown as a sign it's real, and learn stop, check, ask, and never to send a
  password or code. Typical width (Years 7 and 8): mark a made-up inbox Safe or
  Report, checking where links really go."
time: 35
timing: Engage and Explore 10 min · Explain 10 min · Elaborate 8 min · Evaluate 7 min
goals:
  - I can spot hurry, a prize I didn't enter, and 'everyone has it'.
  - I can explain why pressure to hurry means slow down.
  - I can say why I never send a password or code to anyone.
struggle: Students feel embarrassed at the thought of being tricked. Say that
  tricks are designed to work on everyone, adults included; spotting the push is
  a skill, not a test of being clever.
before: >
  **⚑ Wellbeing review:** this course is a draft. Share this lesson and these
  notes with the school's wellbeing lead before teaching, and agree the support
  pathway and any local wording.


  **If a student discloses something:** follow the school's child-protection
  procedure. Listen, don't probe, don't promise to keep it secret, and pass it
  on as the procedure says. Thank them and steer the class back to Leo and
  Grace. A student who has lost money or an account may feel ashamed: reassure
  them that telling was right.


  **Ground rules:** Leo, Grace, Ava and every message are made up; addresses use
  `.example`. Don't ask whether students have been tricked, have bought things
  in games, or what games they play. The closing think is private.


  No laws or consumer rules are stated. For reporting scams, point families to
  the eSafety Commissioner (esafety.gov.au) or the school's process.


  The board (Years 7 and 8) is the `cyber` widget's easy inbox from How
  computers work › Spot the phish, which teaches phishing in more depth. Years 5
  and 6: give the link with `?width=minimum`.
running:
  - "Engage: ask whether a real prize would vanish in 60 seconds."
  - "Explore: list the three pushes on the board."
  - "Explain: practise 'Stop, check, ask' with a made-up pop-up."
  - "Elaborate (Years 7 and 8): ask why the link text and where it goes can
    differ."
  - "Evaluate: ask which push the shoe ad used (two of them)."
stuck:
  - see: A student says they'd just click to see if it's real.
    ask: What does the message want you to do first?
    fix: Clicking is what it wants. Close it, and check another way.
  - see: A student thinks giving the password is fine if they change it later.
    ask: What could someone do with it in one minute?
    fix: Passwords and codes are only typed into the real app, never sent.
  - see: A student says something like this has happened to them.
    ask: (Don't probe.) Thank them; say telling someone was the right move.
    fix: Follow up privately; involve parents or the wellbeing team as the school's
      process says.
stretch: Find the push in an ad you make up yourself, then rewrite it with no
  push at all. What changed?
support: "A card: Hurry? Prize I didn't enter? Everyone has it? Then: Stop, check, ask."
leads: >
  Next: when something goes wrong. Stop, keep it, tell, block and report.


  Links: How computers work › Spot the phish (Years 7 and 8; checking links and
  sender addresses).
exit:
  q: A message says you have 1 minute to claim a prize. What do you do?
  a: "Slow down: stop, check where it's from (did I enter?), and ask a trusted
    adult before clicking. Never send a password or code."
explain: >
  Some messages are built to make you act before you think: **hurry**, **a prize
  you didn't enter**, **everyone has it**.


  Pressure to hurry is the sign to **slow down**: **Stop. Check. Ask.**


  Never send a password or a code to anyone. Nobody real minds you checking.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Grace lost her account. She says, 'I'm so stupid, I can't tell anyone.' What
      would you say to her?
    prompts:
      - Who designed the trick, and who was it designed to work on?
      - What could telling someone fix?
    notes: Tricks are designed to work on everyone. Telling early means the account
      can often be recovered. Lesson 7 picks this up.
  activities:
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Name the push
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Your teacher reads made-up messages aloud. Hold up one finger for hurry,
        two for a prize you didn't enter, three for everyone has it, a fist for
        no push.
      notes: Keep messages made up and harmless (game skins, stickers, shoes). Mix in
        a couple with no push.
    - at: investigate
      kind: activity
      title: Stop, check, ask
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        Say it together, with a hand movement for each: Stop (hand up), Check
        (point to eyes), Ask (point to a trusted adult).
      notes: A movement helps younger classes remember. Optional for Years 7 and 8.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Passwords
      type: question
      q: Who should you send your password to?
      options:
        - "Nobody: type it only into the real app or site"
        - A friend you trust
        - The game's support team if they message you
      answer: 0
      explain: Real support never asks for your password in a message.
```

# Grace's thinking for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the line, nothing runs.

# region: grace
A message in Grace's game says she has won a rare pet, but only if she claims it in 5 minutes.
She thinks: it has a countdown, so it must be real and I have to be quick.
She clicks the link and types in her game username and password.
The next day she can't sign in to her account.
# endregion
